title: [Netflix] Ontology-Driven Observability: Building an End-to-End Knowledge Graph at Netflix Scale
summary: Prasanna Vijayanathan, Renzo Sanchez-SilvaWhen Jake Paul and Mike Tyson stepped into the ring in November 2024, we delivered the fight to roughly 65 million concurrent streams. On an ordinary day our infrastructure takes in more than 2 billion requests and handles upwards of 38 million real-time logging events every second. At that scale, the whole picture doesn’t fit into a single engineering team’s head or onto a single dashboard. With more Live content, Podcasts and real-time streams, our need to understand and update our systems as quickly as possible becomes imperative to provide a good user experience. Understanding the system at this scale and within the time constraints we have, often becomes a daunting exercise in finding a needle in a haystack, in a dark jungle, blindfolded.This post is about that search for the needle.The Four hours before a fixConsider a regression of the kind we see in a given week. The home screen where you see the list of lists of movies, starts taking about 1.5 seconds longer to render. An alert fires. And then we go looking for what caused this issue and how do we fix it?As it so happens, a regression on the application could be related to anywhere in the system — a client app regression from a new version deployment or A/B test rollout, a load shedding in the infrastructure, a GraphQL query responding with bad data because of a service rollout 6 hops downstream, are all suspects at this point. So, answering “what caused the issue?” needs insights from across the system, and this involves combing through layers of data in a meticulous manner.The MELT Layer“What caused the issue?”Metrics, events, logs and traces, or MELT, in the industry’s shorthand, are the right raw materials for such an investigation, and each of them answers roughly a quarter of the question. We collect observability data across these four pillars, unified into a single observability data layer. This lets us observe our systems in real time, across what our users are experiencing, how our applications are doing and what our backend infrastructure and services are processing and responding to.MELT — Metrics, Events, Logs and Traces, and how they are captured across the system.The investigation that follows may look like this in each layer:What each layer of MELT tells us and what it leaves outThe timeline of an investigationSo how long does it take to investigate an issue, figure out the root cause and fix it, so our users stop running into this issue again?A timeline of an investigation: ~4 hoursIn our chosen example, four hours. Very little of it went into computing anything difficult. Most of it went into reconstructing relationships that our observability systems already knew but we had never written down anywhere a human or machine could simply read and discover.The disagreement underneathThe instinct here could have been, around 2023, to reach for more data or better dashboards, and while both help at the margins, neither addresses what makes these investigations slow.It’s 2026 now, so we might say, “hey, agents”, but without the right context delivered to the agents, AI systems hallucinate, and especially when teams are on-call and need a fix “now”, we cannot let inaccurate agentic analysis lead us down the wrong path. We need the right needle, not any needle.Each of our systems is internally coherent and externally isolated. Atlas, our telemetry platform, knows applications and their time series. Radar, our alerting system, knows thresholds and firing history. incident.io knows severities and responders. PagerDuty knows rotations. Spinnaker knows what shipped and when. And our Slack history knows, in a form no query engine can reach, which engineer solved something very similar last quarter and what they found.The difficulty is that they do not agree on what they are talking about. A thing that is an application in one system is a service in a second and a cluster in a third, with names differing by a suffix, a casing convention, or a rename only a couple of people remember (SMEs, ring a bell?). Joining across them requires a human carrying the mapping in their head, and that person becomes the bottleneck in such cross-domain investigations. The hard part of end-to-end observability is probably better understood as a data modelling problem.What we lacked was an explicit, machine-readable agreement about the entities in our operational world.The OntologyThis agreement has a name: an ontology. Ontology is a formal specification of types, the properties they carry, and the relationships they may have. Its unit is the triple, one fact expressed as subject, predicate, object. Consider the following example triples.api-gateway rdf:type ops:Application .api-gateway ops:ownedBy "Team Bedrock" .api-gateway ops:deployedIn "us-east-1" .INC-5377 rdf:type ops:Incident .INC-5377 ops:affects api-gateway .INC-5377 ops:severity "SEV 2" .In the example here, we have already encoded six facts, and can answer in one query, a question that used to span three tools.“Which incidents affected applications owned by Team Bedrock in us-east-1?” is a single query in place of looking up incidents, Spinnaker and Radar.We call our ontology layer, The Observability Ontology. It acts as the schema, rule set and shared agreement that standardizes how different systems understand entities like applications, services, incidents, deployments, etc.We built it on the W3C stack for this: RDF for the data model, OWL for the ontology, SHACL for validation, and SPARQL for querying. These standards are well specified and widely implemented, which keeps the model portable across graph stores.The data from the ontology itself, is stored as a knowledge graph, persisted to QuipuDB, our homegrown RDF graph database, a distributed quad store based on redb, a Rust-based embedded key value db. Data here is generated by parsing raw telemetry, logs, and incident discussions into triples (subject-predicate-object facts).Every harvest also produces a full Turtle serialization for archival, making it human-readable and diff-friendly, which has proven more useful for debugging than we expected.Our ontology is organized into twelve namespaces, each owning one operational domain:There are two decisions about this ontology that mattered while we built it, so they’re worth sharing.The first is that we refused a generic Service type. “Service” means four different things across our tooling, so applications resolve to exactly one type, ops:Application, and every one of them is validated against our software catalog of roughly 49,000 entries before the entity is created. Unvalidated strings like usernames, team names, dependency names scraped from network topology, never become applications. We also cap dependency edges in both directions, because one popular service can carry thousands of reverse dependencies and would otherwise dominate the graph.The second decision concerns what we chose to model. Incident chat carries the reasoning behind an incident. The hypotheses tried and discarded, the mitigation that worked, who knew why, is all context in the incident’s Slack channel and that knowledge evaporates when the channel goes quiet. So a 200-message, 50-person, 15-service incident channel becomes a structure, converting the operational chaos of an incident into ordered triples:Creating determinism from non-determinismBuilding this graph means using tools that are inherently stochastic. LLMs summarize discussions. Fuzzy matching resolves service names. A probabilistic engine proposes causal chains. None of these produce the same output twice with certainty, but what comes out at the end of our system is a deterministic graph that answers a SPARQL query the same way every time.The ontology is the mechanism that creates this determinism through its pipelined approach. We think of the pipeline as a ladder that drives entropy down, where entropy means the proportion of information still trapped in unstructured form. For example, at the start of this pipeline, an LLM could say anything, but it cannot emit a triple that violates the type system. We constrain the output space tightly enough and a stochastic process yields a deterministic contract:# The model may produce any prose. Its output MUST fit these predicates:category IN sentiment IN # Result — a deterministic triple:thread:123 slack:category "incident" .thread:123 slack:isIncidentRelated "true"^^xsd:boolean .There are five layers that get us down this ladder. Any single step of this ladder is non-deterministic. But in aggregate, the chain becomes deterministic. That inversion is the whole trick. We describe them below:The five layers to create determinism from non-determinismEnrichers: Agents as entropy reducersWe use what we call, enrichers, to reduce entropy across the knowledge graph. Dozens of enrichers run over the graph. Each one of them takes noisy input and emits typed triples, and each reads what earlier enrichers wrote. The contract for an Enricher is deliberately narrow:class Enricher: async def _enrich_async(self, ...): raw = await self.fetch(...) # 1. read noisy input result = self.analyze(raw) # 2. process (may be stochastic) graph.add((uri, RDF.type, OPS.X)) # 3. emit TYPED triples graph.add((uri, OPS.pred, Literal(result.value))) return EnrichmentResult(success=True, triples_added=count)Three invariants that are standard across the enrichers:every entity carries an rdf:type,every URI follows a single naming scheme, andthe catalog gates every ops:Application.Two operational choices are worth naming here, as well. The enrichment pipeline runs sequentially — load the graph, add triples, and save.This sequencing removes an entire category of race conditions at a cost in wall-clock time we are happy to pay. And calls out to external systems like metrics, logs, events and the rest could be best-effort, so a slow downstream API doesn’t block the graph harvest, albeit some degradation. To that end, we are also working to translate these separate systems into the ontology, such as the Metrics Ontology and the Alerts Ontology, so everything could be queried from the Ontology itself.The Correlation Engine: finding the correlation chainsThe correlation engine assimilates the vast number of signals from diverse input sources and condenses them into causal or correlatory chains of events. Today, the engine reads thirteen signal types, including log errors, metric anomalies, slow and failed traces, alerts, incidents, deployments, config changes, experiments, autoscaling, commits, end-to-end bottlenecks, and error patterns. It then searches for paths among them. Some ordered pairs are known to be causal and carry a high prior weight. For example, deployment before log error, config change before metric anomaly, failed trace before incident, and so on. Others, which show high correlation are considered correlation chains. Such chains are scored on temporal proximity and severity, inside a ten-minute window, with anything under 0.6 confidence getting discarded.The Correlation EngineThe role of the engine here is to propose with evidence, not to make conclusions. Hence, the engine stores its chains along with the graph records that were used to create them.A 0.87 chain in the above example, is a strong hypothesis for a human or an agent to check, and the graph records the confidence alongside the claim so that consumers can understand why a chain is what it is and weigh their options to make decisions.The knowledge flywheelEach harvest cycle turns the same four steps, and each rotation leaves the graph richer for the next. This is the Knowledge Flywheel, leading to continuous enrichment and improvement of the context about our system, stored in the knowledge graph.The Knowledge FlywheelObserve collects the signals. Enrich adds typed triples. Infer finds patterns invisible in the raw data. Adapt feeds knowledge back, so that established patterns become detection rules. The compounding result of the four phases leads to a self-improving system. A causal chain discovered in one incident becomes a known pattern for the next, and the ontology gradually stops being a schema and starts being a memory.Consider the example above. When we first see an incident in api-gateway caused due to a timeout and resolve it, we convert this knowledge into entries to the ontology. This becomes encoded knowledge. As we go through multiple cycles of this encoding, the graph starts learning patterns. After N cycles, patterns become wisdom — “api-gateway deploys cause 40% of SEV-2s” and “30% of deployment issues in api-gateway come from Connection Timeouts”. Surface this as an insight and we proactively start reducing incidents, not just react quickly to new ones.Putting the graph to workOn top of the graph sits AutoRCA, our internal agentic AI solution, built with a set of specialist agents coordinated around one question. Walking the home page regression from the top of this post, the agentic system’s reasoning chain might look something like this:Each specialization to the inputs is built by people who understand their respective domain deeply. That division of labour only works if the specialists can pass findings to one another without having to agree on the terms of communication or even have knowledge of each other. The ontology acts as the interface. Each specialist learns one vocabulary — the graph’s. A team writing specialized use cases for how they use traces record their findings as triples about an ops:Application, the logs specialization reads triples about that same ops:Application, and neither needs to know the other exists. A new specialist learns the same vocabulary once and can immediately read everything the other six have written.Set against the investigation we opened with, the change is narrower than it might sound. The alert still fires at 3:30pm, an engineer still has to weigh the evidence, and the fix still has to be written by someone who understands the code. The hour or two that used to go into assembling context — finding the owning team, reconstructing what shipped, correlating information from different parts of the system, recalling that something similar happened last quarter — all that work is the part the ontology and the graph absorbs. We are early enough that the ranked hypotheses are sometimes wrong, which is why each one carries the evidence that produced it. But when the engineer now starts the investigation, they are already holding the picture that used to take half an afternoon to assemble.If you want to build one of theseA fair amount of what we have built, we learned by getting it wrong first. Based on this experience, these are the principles we would carry into a second attempt.Model identity before anything else. Choose one authoritative catalog per entity kind and validate against it before creating an entity.Treat the ontology as code. Version it, review it, test it, and let changes arrive as pull requests. Treating the ontology as code lends itself to agentic development and lets teams scale and contribute to it.Separate concepts from instances. Concepts change on a human timescale and instances change continuously, conflating them makes both harder to evolve.Build on open standards. RDF, OWL, SHACL and SPARQL are specified, implemented many times over, and portable. A bespoke graph model ties a future consumer to one implementation.Constrain stochastic tools with a type system. This is the principle we would defend hardest. Models are useful precisely where determinism is impossible, and a sufficiently narrow output contract converts their output into something a query engine can trust.Make enrichment best-effort and ordered. A slow dependency should utmost degrade the graph, never block it. And ordering enrichers so each builds on the last buys more accuracy and that’s worth the tradeoff with parallelism that buys speed.Model human reasoning alongside machine telemetry. The most valuable edges in our graph came from discussion. Telemetry records what the system did, discussion records what people understood and interpreted. The reasoning is more valuable to store and serve as wisdom when we need it.Keep humans as the approvers. Let agents propose fixes, enrichers, and ontology changes, and route every proposal through a review process with humans in the loop.What comes nextThe graph makes three things possible. First, automatic root cause analysis, where a regression arrives with a ranked set of graph-backed hypotheses attached. Next, automated remediation, where a sufficiently confident diagnosis carries a proposed action like a targeted rollback, a traffic shift, a code change. And eventually infrastructure that heals itself, acting on a predicted failure before members feel it.Alongside this, we plan to integrate the Observability Ontology with Upper, the domain-modeling language at the heart of Netflix’s Unified Data Architecture (UDA). Upper lets teams describe business and system domains as interconnected, machine-readable models and preserve their meaning and constraints as those models are projected into concrete schemas and systems. This integration would connect operational concepts such as applications, alerts, deployments, and incidents to the broader set of domains modeled across Netflix, giving engineers and agents a shared semantic layer for querying, validation, and reasoning. We will begin with a proof of concept that models incidents in Upper and use what we learn to determine where the two systems should converge.AcknowledgementsNone of this would exist without the teams who share their data, expertise, and patience with an early system. We want to specially acknowledge the efforts of our own team members who made this possible from very early on in this lifecycle, Kaela Marsheck and Aditya Gaur. We are also especially grateful to our collaborators in Netflix’s ontology working group, Peter Royal, Alex Hutter, and to Alexandre Bertails and members of the Unified Data Architecture (UDA)/Knowledge Foundations team for sharing Upper and their domain-modeling expertise, and for helping us explore how the Observability Ontology can become part of a broader semantic foundation at Netflix.Ontology-Driven Observability: Building an End-to-End Knowledge Graph at Netflix Scale was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: [Amazon AWS] AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities is now generally available
summary: Today, we’re announcing the general availability of AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities. AWS Continuum is a security service that finds and validates code vulnerabilities, then delivers fixes as patches you can automate or as pull requests in your repositories. AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities confirms which findings are exploitable in your environment, ranks the resulting issues by business impact, and proposes a fix for each one. Every remediation starts in a mode where Continuum proposes the fix and a person approves it before it ships. In the future, you will be able to decide which actions Continuum can take on its own, within the guardrails you define. Using frontier artificial intelligence (AI) models, threat actors can turn a vulnerability disclosure into working exploit code in minutes, and the same tools that speed up development also increase the volume of findings your teams must process. If your organization runs a large application estate, your scanners likely produce thousands of findings a day, and many of them need no action. A finding can be unreachable, unexploitable, or already mitigated by a runtime control. Generic severity scores don’t tell you which resources a threat actor can actually reach, so a critical score on a dev-only utility looks the same as a medium score on a service one step away from a payments database. Previously, confirming whether a finding was exploitable took hours of manual investigation, and shipping a fix with confidence took days of coordination across security, infrastructure, and application teams, because the blast radius of a change is hard to assess without business context. To close that gap, Continuum proves which findings are exploitable and bounds the risk of each fix it proposes. Continuum builds a context graph from two primary sources: your code repositories and your AWS environment. For AWS, you set up a collector in the account and Region where your code runs. The collector gathers resource details such as AWS Config resources and network configuration so Continuum can judge whether a vulnerability is reachable over the network and what a threat actor could reach from it. From this graph, Continuum learns which systems are business-critical, who owns them, how services depend on one another, and which data each one touches. It uses that picture to identify your highest-value systems, such as customer data stores, payment pipelines, and authentication services, and then ranks each resulting issue by how close its attack path runs to those systems. Continuum analyzes each finding against your code and its environment context and assigns an evidence level, such as a verdict proven by static analysis of the vulnerable code path. For findings it can reproduce, Continuum runs the exploit in an isolated sandbox and attaches proof-of-concept code with the reproduction steps. It produces the attack path, the supporting source analysis, and a blast radius assessment instead of a risk score alone. It also evaluates whether your existing defenses would detect and stop the validated path. For each confirmed issue, Continuum generates a fix (a code patch, a dependency upgrade, or a configuration change) and opens it as a pull request in your connected repository, ready to review. Every fix requires human approval: you review and merge the pull request, so the final decision stays with your team. In the future, you will be able to build confidence in specific remediation classes and let Continuum apply those fixes automatically once its confidence gates pass, such as test coverage, scope bounds, and historical success rate. AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities in action To show how this works, I open AWS Continuum in the console and go to Code vulnerabilities. Before I can review issues, I set up an environment. I connect a code source, either a GitHub integration or an Amazon S3 bucket, and then create an environment that scans it on a schedule I choose. An Amazon S3 source has a couple of prerequisites: the bucket sits in the same account and AWS Region where I turn on AWS Continuum, and I grant access through an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role that AWS Continuum assumes. I can optionally add AWS infrastructure context by setting up an AWS Continuum collector in the account and Region where my code runs and authorizing my environment to use it. For the full requirements and steps, see the AWS Continuum User Guide. The Overview page brings these pieces together in one place, showing my Code integrations, the Environments built on them, and the status of any AWS collector that supplies AWS resource context. I open one of my environments. The Issues tab lists validated, prioritized issues rather than raw scanner output, each with a severity, a status, and the time it was created. I choose one of the issues. The Overview rates it High severity, with the status Completed and the remediation already Delivered to GitHub. The Risk assessment explains why. Continuum rates its Exploitability as Exploitable, with an evidence level of Static proven and a validation run status of Completed. Likelihood is High, since the service is reachable from an attacker, requires no authentication, and needs no user interaction. Impact is Moderate, which means an attacker gains the ability to modify business data, with a blast radius reaching other users in the same tenant. A Proof section includes the source analysis behind the verdict. The Remediation section shows a fix already delivered as a pull request in GitHub, changing four files, with 50 lines added and 24 removed across the cart service. Continuum opens the fix as a pull request titled Continuum fix, and I choose View pull request to open it in GitHub. The console is explicit that a generated patch does not mean the issue is fixed. I still review and merge it, which keeps the final decision with my team. A Contributing findings section lists the specific scanner finding this issue was built from. The pull request description carries the same risk assessment, remediation summary, and proof from the console, so whoever reviews it in GitHub sees the evidence without leaving their workflow. The Findings tab lists the raw scanner findings across the environment, the evidence that issues are built from. The Scans tab shows the history of each scan with its status, origin, and request and completion times, and I use Configure scan frequency to change the cadence or Queue scan to run one on demand. The Configuration tab is where I manage the environment: the code and context sources it reads from, its code integrations, environment settings such as whether Continuum creates remediation patches, and the AWS collectors it uses for AWS context. In a single workflow, I work through the validated issues in priority order with each scan, reviewing the evidence and scope behind each one before I approve and merge the fixes I trust. Every fix waits for my approval, so the backlog keeps shrinking while my team keeps control of what ships. Now available AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities is available today in US East (N. Virginia) and US West (Oregon) Regions. For pricing, visit the pricing page. To learn more, visit the AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities product page and the User Guide. Give it a try in the AWS Continuum console today, and send us feedback through your usual AWS Support contacts. — Esra

title: [HashiCorp] Announcing the public preview of HashiCorp Vault Arc: Evolve security for emerging workloads
summary: Enterprises rely on HashiCorp Vault to secure access to sensitive systems, applications, and data across increasingly complex hybrid and multi-cloud environments. But the environment around those applications is changing. Machine identities continue to grow, certificate lifecycles are becoming shorter, cryptographic requirements are evolving, and AI agents are creating a new class of autonomous workload that must be identified, authorized, and governed. Today, we are announcing the public preview of Vault Arc, expanding the Vault portfolio with new capabilities designed for these emerging security and operational requirements. Vault Arc is still Vault. It builds on the role Vault plays in enterprise security while introducing a new approach to how security resources are modeled, governed, queried, and operated. Importantly, Vault Arc complements Vault Enterprise rather than requiring customers to replace it. Organizations can continue deploying and expanding Vault Enterprise for existing and new workloads while evaluating Vault Arc where its capabilities provide additional value. Extending Vault for what's next Modernization isn't simply about replacing existing technology. It's about giving organizations the flexibility to respond as their infrastructure, workloads, and security requirements change. Vault Arc introduces a resource-based approach to Security Lifecycle Management. Security resources can be represented with unique resource identities designed to make them easier to understand, query, govern, and incorporate into security policy. This approach provides a foundation for several important capabilities: More intuitive authorization and governance. Vault Arc separates access grants from broader governance policies, helping organizations establish enterprise guardrails while allowing teams to manage appropriate access within those boundaries. Greater visibility and auditability. Typed, queryable resources make it easier for security and platform teams to understand what exists in their environment and answer questions about credentials and other security resources. Simplified operations and developer workflows. Vault Arc is designed to reduce operational complexity while making common workflows easier to consume through APIs, automation, and streamlined user experiences. Cryptographic agility. As cryptographic standards evolve, Vault Arc provides a foundation for more policy-driven approaches to managing keys, certificates, algorithms, and future cryptographic transitions. Preparing for machine and agentic workloads The growth of non-human identities is changing what enterprises need from identity and secrets management. AI agents accelerate that change. Agents can perform different tasks, interact with multiple tools and systems, and take actions on behalf of people and applications. The authority an agent requires can therefore depend on its identity, current task, context, and mandate. Treating these agents simply as another long-lived service account risks losing that context. Vault Arc is being designed with these emerging workloads in mind. The public preview establishes capabilities for agent identity governance, scoped and ephemeral authorization, and auditable agent activity. Organizations can begin moving toward a model in which agent access is tied more closely to identity, policy, and the work being performed. This represents an important step toward Agentic Security Lifecycle Management (SLM), where organizations can govern what an agent represents, what it is authorized to do, what credentials and resources it can access, and what actions it performs throughout its lifecycle. Modernization without a forced migration Vault Enterprise and Vault Arc are designed to coexist, giving organizations the flexibility to determine where each best meets their requirements. Customers can continue deploying Vault Enterprise while evaluating and adopting Vault Arc incrementally based on individual applications, workloads, and use cases. This approach allows modernization to happen at the pace of the enterprise rather than according to an arbitrary migration deadline. Organizations can progressively evaluate and introduce new capabilities while reducing the disruption and risk traditionally associated with major platform transitions. Extending governance across Vault As organizations expand their Vault footprint, they also need greater visibility and governance across an increasingly distributed security estate. Secure Hub, also entering public preview, complements this strategy by providing centralized visibility, reporting, and governance across Vault environments, including Vault Enterprise and Vault Arc. This gives organizations greater enterprise-wide context while controls and enforcement remain within individual Vault environments. Together, Vault Arc and Secure Hub provide organizations with greater flexibility to introduce new capabilities while developing a more consistent governance model across their broader Vault estate. Expanding security lifecycle management Together with Vault Enterprise, Secure Hub, and capabilities across the broader IBM security portfolio, Vault Arc advances a Security Lifecycle Management strategy designed for environments in which humans, applications, machines, and increasingly autonomous agents all require secure access to enterprise resources. The public preview gives customers an opportunity to experience that direction firsthand and provide feedback that helps shape the evolution of Vault Arc. Join the HashiCorp Vault Arc public preview to explore the new capabilities, share your feedback, and evaluate how Secure Hub can extend your organization's Security Lifecycle Management strategy. Learn more about the SLM announcements at TechXchange.

title: [CNCF] We organized Sustainability Month. Here’s what we learned. 🌱
summary: What do Kubernetes resource allocation, eBPF, carbon observability, and GPUs have in common? Quite a lot, actually. Especially when you start looking at them through the lens of environmental sustainability. This October, we brought these conversations together as part of Cloud Native Sustainability Month. And while the idea was to help our community learn more about sustainability, we ended up learning quite a few things ourselves. But first, a little backstory. How did we get here? It all started in 2023, when the CNCF TAG Environmental Sustainability launched the first Cloud Native Sustainability Week. The idea was simple: bring cloud native communities together to explore how technology can become more environmentally sustainable. What began as a week of events eventually grew into a month-long initiative, with sustainability efforts continuing under CNCF TAG Operational Resilience. Fast-forward to October 2026, and communities were once again bringing their own perspectives to the conversation. In Bucharest, we joined the initiative with a virtual meetup featuring speakers from across the cloud native ecosystem. Our goal? Make sustainability a little less abstract and a lot more relevant to the engineering decisions we make every day. So, what did we learn? 1. Sustainability is closer to our everyday work than we think. When someone mentions environmental sustainability in tech, it’s easy to think about carbon emissions, renewable energy, or data centers. But what about the resources we allocate to Kubernetes workloads? The CPU cycles we consume? Or that extra GPU we’re considering adding to our infrastructure? Our speakers approached sustainability from different angles, and that’s what made the discussions interesting. We explored carbon observability with OpenTelemetry, energy metrics, Kubernetes resource allocation, eBPF, GPU efficiency, and even how data center efficiency is calculated. Different topics, but a common thread: sometimes, making technology more sustainable starts with questioning how we use the resources we already have. And that’s something most of us can relate to. 2. You don’t need to be a sustainability expert to join the conversation. This one applies to attendees, speakers, and organizers alike. Sustainability is a big topic. There’s a lot to learn, and honestly, it can be a little intimidating when you don’t know where to start. But that’s exactly why community events matter. You don’t need to understand every aspect of carbon accounting to ask whether your workloads are using resources efficiently. And you don’t need years of experience in sustainable computing to share an experiment or ask a good question. Sometimes, a lightning talk about something you’ve been working on is enough to get others thinking. And sometimes, the most interesting conversations start with someone saying, “Have you considered trying this?” 3. Organizing is a learning experience, too. We usually think about events from the attendees’ perspective. What will they learn? Which talks will they find interesting? Will they leave with something useful? But there’s another side to it. As organizers, we get to discover projects, connect with speakers, and explore topics we might not otherwise encounter. Of course, there’s also the less glamorous part: making sure everything comes together—and yes, sometimes wondering whether anyone will actually show up. And yes, sometimes wondering whether anyone will actually show up. But seeing people come together around a shared interest makes the effort worthwhile. One thing we’ve come to appreciate is that you don’t need a huge conference or an elaborate program to create something valuable. A few good talks, curious people, and a topic worth discussing can go a long way. The event is over. Now what? One of the challenges with sustainability is figuring out what to do after the conversation ends. The good news? There are plenty of ways to get involved. If you’re an engineer, start by looking at how efficiently your applications use resources. Explore projects like Kepler, a CNCF incubating project, and experiment with energy metrics or share something you’ve learned. If you’re interested in open source, there are opportunities to contribute through code, documentation, testing, and community discussions. And if you’re a community organizer, why not bring sustainability into your next meetup? You don’t need to dedicate an entire event to it. Start with a lightning talk, invite someone working on an interesting project, or organize a discussion around a problem your community is already facing. Small steps count, too. See you in 2027? Looking back, organizing Sustainability Month reminded us of something we already love about the cloud native community: there’s always someone willing to share what they know, and someone else curious enough to learn. We certainly don’t have all the answers about making cloud native technology more sustainable. But we have a community that’s willing to ask questions, experiment, and figure things out together. And that’s a pretty good place to start. So, if you’re part of a cloud native community and have been thinking about organizing something for Sustainability Month 2027, consider this your invitation. Bring your ideas, your questions, and your community. We’ll figure out the rest together. 🌱

title: [Cloudflare] See the agents, set the terms: new visibility and control for personal agents
summary: Personal agents are the intermediary between humans and the Internet, turning a person’s instructions into requests and actions on websites. A customer might ask a personal agent to compare products across your site, find support articles, or complete a purchase. To a site owner, all three interactions show up as automated traffic — and without a clear view of which agents are visiting and what they are doing, it can be difficult to know whether that traffic is helping your business or creating risk. Blocking agents altogether can feel like the safest choice, but it can mean losing customers. Better visibility into agent activity allows you to decide what access makes sense for your site.Today, we’re launching new analytics to help you understand how personal agents access your site on behalf of humans, along with more granular access policies to put those decisions into practice. Together, they let you welcome agents on your own terms, and in ways that support your business.See how agents access your siteKnowing which agent is behind a request turns unexplained automated traffic into traffic you can act on with confidence. Cloudflare maintains the largest verified bot directory in the world, and we are now bringing that intelligence into your traffic details. In Security Analytics, the Bot Analysis chart now shows Personal Assistants as a new category, next to Verified Bot, Likely Human, Likely Automated, and Automated. Security teams can select it to see only personal agent traffic over time.In Top statistics, a new Personal Assistants widget lists which agents are visiting your site and how many requests each one sends. Filter on one agent and every other widget updates to show only its traffic details: the paths it requests, the status codes it receives, and the networks it comes from. At a glance, you can see whether an agent is logging in, reading your product pages, reaching your checkout, or hitting errors on pages it cannot use.For sites that protect user accounts with Account Abuse Protection (currently in early access), site owners and fraud teams are able to see which user each agent represents. The population overview page shows which personal agents are active across your users and how many accounts use them, so you can determine whether agent traffic is a meaningful part of your business. Every login and sign-up event now shows whether a personal agent made the request, and which one. Fraud teams can filter accounts by AI assistant events or number of AI assistants.Additionally, each user's account overview shows the agents acting for that account. A fraud analyst investigating an unusual login can tell whether it came from an agent the customer has relied on for weeks, or from an agent that appeared for the first time today and needs a closer look. If it looks like an attacker is using an agent on an account, fraud analysts can mitigate that account directly, with a WAF rule on its Hashed User ID, without blocking the agent for everyone else who relies on it.Together, these views give you a clearer basis for deciding which personal agents to welcome, limit, or block.Set access policies that reflect your preferencesWe introduced AI bot policies this summer so site owners could make separate access control choices for AI bots used for Search, Training, and Agent behaviors. Now we’re expanding the existing Agents policy to include granular control options for supported personal agents. To reflect this broader scope, we’re renaming the setting AI Crawler and Agent access policies.In Security Settings, you can set an overall Agents policy, then choose a different policy for each supported personal agent: Allow (do not block), Block on pages with ads, or Block. For example, you can set the overall Agents policy to Block on pages with ads, then choose Allow (do not block) for a supported personal agent you want to welcome. Your existing Search and Training policies stay as they are.You can also make these choices when you add a new zone to Cloudflare. During onboarding, we ask whether you monetize pages with ads and then tailor the recommended policies to your answer. You can always revisit your access controls later in Security Settings.The right policy depends on your site. One publisher may allow a supported personal agent throughout its site so readers can find its articles, while another may block that same agent on pages where ads support the content. Both publishers are choosing the access control that works for their business.Agent identity is only part of the storyThe analytics and policies we’re launching today give site owners visibility into personal agent activity and control over their access. Our next goal is to help site owners preserve the context of their relationships with users when personal agents act as intermediaries. A site may recognize the agent making a request but lack information it would otherwise have about the user: whether they are an existing customer, what they authorized the agent to do, whether they have a subscription, or which protections should apply.Reaching that goal will require privacy-aware ways to (1) carry user context through an agent, (2) help sites assess reputation, and (3) establish clear accountability when something goes wrong. We’ll be sharing more as we work with agent operators and others across the ecosystem, so site owners can choose whether to grant agents greater access while continuing to build relationships with their users. Make the choice for your siteThat person asking a personal agent to compare products, find support, or complete a purchase is still a customer trying to reach your business. Review how personal agents are accessing your site, then visit Security Settings → AI Crawler and Agent access policies to set the terms that work for your site.

title: [Dropbox Tech] Evolving our calendar assistant Reclaim to be AI-native without starting over
summary: Calendars hold more than just blocks of time. They reflect how people plan their days, coordinate with others, and make room for what matters to them. Reclaim, the Dropbox-owned calendar assistant, helps manage that complexity by using AI to find and adjust time for tasks, habits, and meetings. That approach works well when inputs and expected outcomes are clear. But people also use Reclaim for scheduling that’s less straightforward. As AI assistants and natural-language interfaces became more capable, they opened up a new way for people to use Reclaim. We imagined situations where users could describe a scheduling goal in their own words, even when it didn’t map neatly to an existing setting or command. Words alone wouldn’t be enough to determine what should happen on a real calendar, though. Reclaim still needs the context that gives requests meaning, including what’s already scheduled, when a user is available, and which preferences and commitments impact changes. Connecting natural-language requests with the surrounding calendar context could help people spend less time figuring out which settings or actions to use. But building the experience required more than adding an AI interface to the existing product. We needed to rethink how Reclaim turned conversational requests into calendar changes while preserving the scheduling system already in place. Evolving Reclaim for AI without starting over For our engineers, the rebuild started with the way Reclaim already managed calendars. Calendar changes carry real weight because time is precious and scheduled events often involve other people. Any new AI capability needed to feel like a natural extension of Reclaim, and it needed to work with the scheduling logic already in place. Before the redesign, Reclaim handled calendar changes in two primary ways. Users could make specific changes themselves, like moving an event or updating a setting. And Reclaim’s automated scheduler also worked in the background. It considered each person’s preferences and availability when finding time for tasks, focus work, and recurring routines like lunch, then adjusted those calendar blocks as schedules changed. The emergence of AI agents introduced a potential third way for users to use Reclaim. Instead of choosing a specific setting or command, a user might prefer to describe what they want to do in their own words. An agent could then interpret that request, look at the relevant parts of their calendar, and work out how Reclaim could help. But we needed to address several challenges before introducing agents to the experience. Large language models can interpret the same request in different ways because they generate answers based on patterns in their training data. For example, an open-ended request like “make time for this tomorrow” could lead an agent to find an open block, create a new event, or move something already on the calendar. Each option would affect the user’s schedule differently, and some could affect other people’s calendars, too. That variability made AI agents different from the two paths Reclaim already supported. Although they arrive at decisions differently, all three actors needed to rely on the same scheduling logic. Creating a separate AI-only path would have duplicated functionality and made Reclaim’s behavior harder to keep consistent across interfaces. We needed a system that could connect a model to both the right calendar information and Reclaim capabilities while also controlling how it used them. The result was an agent platform designed to work within Reclaim’s existing architecture. Building the agent platform Our agent platform gives a model relevant calendar details and access to Reclaim’s features while controlling what the model can see and do. The model interprets what the user says and figures out what they want. The agent, meanwhile, manages the larger process by providing Reclaim’s instructions, relevant calendar context, and tools (which let it ask Reclaim to look up information or request a specific action). When a tool returns information, the agent can send it back to the model to inform the next step. This repeated exchange is called the agent loop. As part of this process, Reclaim gives the agent the calendar information and tools relevant to each request, rather than access to everything at once. This helps the agent focus on the immediate task and limits it to the appropriate actions. For a more complex request, the agent can give one specific part to a specialized subagent. Internal checklists and review steps help keep the overall request on track. Ultimately, we opted to build the agent loop, tools, and the system for gathering context ourselves, and we connect directly to model providers instead of relying on a broad agent framework. That’s because a framework we initially explored lagged behind the provider APIs we wanted to use and included more structure than Reclaim needed. Owning these parts lets us design them around Reclaim’s scheduling needs, adopt new provider capabilities more quickly, and work with different model providers without rebuilding the rest of the platform. That leaves us with more code to maintain, though using agents to help with that code offsets some of the additional work. The same tool system supports Model Context Protocol (MCP) in two ways. Inside Reclaim’s agent loop, an MCP client lets the agent use compatible tools from other services. Separately, Reclaim’s MCP server makes selected Reclaim tools available through supported AI clients, including Claude and ChatGPT. Those clients use their own models and agent loops, but can call the same tools used within Reclaim. Our agent platform helped Reclaim work through open-ended requests, but we still needed safeguards around any changes it proposed. Users needed a way to review those changes before they reached their actual calendars. Making calendar changes consistent and reviewable Behind the scenes, Reclaim represents each scheduling capability as a Schedule Action, our internal term for a standard operation like creating or updating an event, changing an RSVP, or finding availability. Whether a request comes from a user, the automated scheduler, or an agent, the same Schedule Action type is used, including the same validation and commit process. That shared path matters because a calendar change can affect more than one event. Moving a meeting might change someone’s availability or cause Reclaim to adjust flexible events elsewhere on a user’s calendar. If each actor used a separate implementation, engineers would have to reproduce those rules and keep every version aligned as Reclaim evolved, which would have become tedious over time. Because all three actors use the same Schedule Action, engineers can change how an operation works in one place rather than updating three separate versions. This helps Reclaim behave consistently across its interfaces. But even when Reclaim handles a change consistently, users still need to see whether its wider effects match what they want to do. That’s why we developed Preview Mode, which gives users a temporary version of their calendar where they can review AI suggestions and changes requested through chat before applying them to their actual calendar. Essentially, they’re able to see how an event or settings change would affect the rest of their schedule before it goes live. They can then confirm that the change behaves as expected and review any effects on shared events before calendar updates are sent to other attendees. To keep Preview Mode fast, we reworked the automated scheduler as a pure function, meaning, in part, that it can calculate a proposed schedule without saving anything to the user’s actual calendar. Reclaim can repeat that calculation whenever the user adjusts the preview. Because busy calendars and meetings with several attendees require a lot of data, Reclaim keeps a readily accessible copy in Redis, a data store designed for fast retrieval. It also updates attendee availability within the preview whenever an event moves, so the next calculation reflects the schedule being proposed. Keeping AI workflows connected Reclaim now has a consistent path from a natural-language request to a reviewed calendar change. The agent platform connects models with relevant calendar information and Reclaim features, Schedule Actions route proposed updates through the product’s scheduling logic, and Preview Mode makes their effects visible before anything reaches the calendar or other attendees. Together, these pieces extend Reclaim with AI while preserving the scheduling experience people already rely on. This work also reinforced what AI needs in order to be useful inside an active workflow. A model needs the surrounding information to understand a request, a controlled way to act on it, and a review step before the result moves forward. In Reclaim, a scheduling goal can move from conversation to a proposed schedule and then to an approved calendar update without requiring the user to translate it into a specific setting or command. The long-term value of this rebuild is the freedom to evolve without fragmenting the product. As AI changes how people ask for help, Reclaim can introduce new capabilities through the same scheduling foundation rather than adding a separate experience each time. For Reclaim, this offers a practical framework for expanding AI-assisted workflows as models improve and people find new ways to manage their time. ~ ~ ~ If building innovative products, experiences, and infrastructure excites you, come build the future with us! title: [Dropbox Tech] Dropbox CTO Ali Dasdan on moving from AI adoption to transformation
summary: As AI becomes a starting point for more kinds of work, its usefulness depends on access to an organization’s trusted knowledge and context, including the files, research, feedback, decisions, and project history that give the work meaning. Dropbox helps people bring that context into the supported AI tools they choose while preserving the permissions and controls they expect, so they can spend less time finding, uploading, and re-explaining what already exists. When AI helps them create something new, Dropbox gives that work a trusted, durable home where it can be saved, shared, reviewed, approved, and built on over time. That focus on connected workflows also shapes how we use AI within Dropbox. Access to increasingly capable models can help teams produce more. But turning that output into sustained gains in productivity, quality, and customer impact requires examining workflows from end to end. That includes addressing new bottlenecks as output grows, adapting the platform that supports development, aligning organization-wide incentives, and measuring whether greater speed and volume lead to better outcomes. AI also increases the importance of human judgment. People still need to choose the right problems, give agents the context they need, evaluate the validity of their output, and remain in control of important decisions and actions. Problem solving, communication, and leadership become critical to turning AI-enabled output into real value. Dropbox Chief Technology Officer Ali Dasdan and Senior Director of Engineering Productivity Uma Namasivayam discuss lessons from deploying AI at company scale, how we assess productivity and ROI, how our progress compares with industry peers, and what organizations need to consider as they move from AI adoption to broader transformation. What have you learned in the last year about driving productivity with AI, not just for engineers but across the wider Dropbox organization? Ali: You have to start with the outcome you’re trying to achieve. Giving people AI tools is only the first step. As people use them, your assumptions get tested and new bottlenecks emerge. Maybe you’re coding faster, but now you have too many code reviews. Or you’re generating significantly more code, which puts additional stress on the tools and infrastructure that support development. If you want AI to have a meaningful impact, you have to look at the workflow end to end and keep adapting it until you’re producing the outcome you actually want. There’s no silver bullet. Uma: You have to approach it with a product mindset. Leadership saying, “You need to start using AI tools,” is good, but that alone won’t drive adoption. You also need ground-up awareness through initiatives like boot camps and show-and-tells that involve people more deeply. And you have to align incentives so managers understand what ROI they’re getting from it. How should companies think about measuring AI productivity and ROI? Ali: If I write 10 lines of code and push them to production, it’s almost impossible to prove those 10 lines were responsible for a certain amount of customer satisfaction or revenue improvement. I might produce a million lines a day, but if it’s the wrong product and customers have no interest in it, then it’s not going to work. The real ROI metrics are outcomes like revenue, cost, customer satisfaction, and retention. Then we look at proxy metrics that connect our output to those outcomes. Are we moving faster, producing more code, running more experiments, and pushing more features? Is the site faster and more reliable? There’s no single metric. The framework we use focuses on speed, effectiveness, quality, and impact, with multiple metrics under each. The industry hasn’t found the full solution yet. How does Dropbox’s AI-driven engineering productivity compare with companies operating at a similar level of technical scale and complexity? Ali: If we define peers as top technology companies we hire from and compete with for talent, we’re seeing very similar problems and metrics. We’re around 70% AI-generated code, and Uber recently shared a number around 70%. They see a need for internal agentic coding solutions, and so do we. They have their own tools, and we have Nova, our internal service for running coding agents. Larger companies have allocated more resources to these problems, while we’re super lean. Despite that, I feel like we’re comparable with that peer group across multiple metrics, including how quickly we adopted AI and reached our targets. Compared with the broader industry, it appears we’re ahead. Uma: The industry looks at pull request throughput, or the rate at which teams complete code changes, as one proxy metric for productivity. It’s not ‌perfect, but our throughput ranks in the top 5% in a custom benchmark of companies with similarly large, complex codebases and engineering systems. We also look at whether moving faster affects quality. Our change failure percentage, which measures how often a deployment leads to degraded performance or failure, is in line with industry peers at the 75th percentile. Our token usage is also among the lowest in that peer group, which could indicate that our teams or systems are operating efficiently. Together, these measures give us a fuller picture of how we’re doing against similar companies. As AI usage grows, how do you decide where additional investment is worthwhile? Ali: AI requires money, and when we talk about AI funding, we’re talking about a large portfolio. There are products used by individual functions, capabilities in tools like Zoom and Slack, company-wide deployments like ChatGPT Enterprise, automation tools, and coding models. We’re seeing benefits. People are fixing tech debt, long-running migration projects are getting finished, and we’re delivering most of the roadmap with fewer resources. But organizations still have to decide which ideas to pursue and when to invest more, often before they can draw a direct line to ROI. That requires domain expertise, the right incentives, and a lot of judgment. We’re still working through it along with the rest of the industry. How should companies determine whether their AI spend is creating real value? Ali: At Dropbox, we’re starting to think less about raw token consumption and more about the engineering value those tokens create. With Nova, for example, we can connect agent usage to actual engineering workflows, validation, and outcomes. That gives us a way to evaluate AI spend based on the engineering work those tokens help produce, rather than simply how many tokens we’re consuming. As AI lowers the cost and effort required to produce software, which human skills become more valuable? Ali: If you look fundamentally at what engineers or computer scientists do, it’s that we know how to solve a problem. That’ll never disappear. AI may help me solve bigger problems or solve them faster, but I still need to provide better context, ask the right questions, judge the validity of the answers, know how to iterate, and give a good spec and problem definition. I also need to understand how a solution fits into the broader system and adapt as the tools change. Problem solving, communication, systems thinking, and judgment become even more important because agents depend on people to guide and evaluate their work. Uma: I would give you three things. One is problem solving, which Ali explained really well. The second is judgment. The next phase of AI could make the cost of engineering almost zero, which makes choosing the right problems and evaluating what AI produces extremely important. The third is leadership. Leaders need to understand people, navigate ambiguity as work changes, bring teams together, communicate clearly, build trust, and make sure incentives are aligned. Those skills won’t go away at all. Their value will only grow. As AI models and agents become more widely available, what’ll distinguish the organizations that use them effectively, and what role can Dropbox play? Ali: Models and agents can be incredibly capable, but they don’t automatically know which information an organization trusts, what decisions have already been made, who has access, or what needs to happen next. Without that context, even a strong model can produce generic or incomplete results. Dropbox can connect supported AI experiences to customer-owned content and context, then give the work AI produces a place to be saved, shared, reviewed, approved, and continued. People still make consequential decisions, while the work keeps moving without losing the sources, history, and collaborators behind it. A year from now, what do you hope AI-enabled work looks like at Dropbox? Uma: This year, we’ve focused heavily on engineering, and we’re now starting to understand the workflows across product, design, and other non-engineering teams. A year from now, the goal is for people across those teams to be able to come up with ideas, test them with customers, and potentially ship some of those features. If our customer experience team sees an issue, for example, they could use agents to develop a solution and see whether it works for the customer. That’s the vision we’re pursuing internally. If we can prove it works, we could potentially enable external customers to build on Dropbox platforms and use AI with the building blocks we have. ~ ~ ~ If building innovative products, experiences, and infrastructure excites you, come build the future with us!
